question: Tens of thousands of people have already disappeared or died at the Union’s external borders whilst fleeing war, persecution and hardship. Often, their bodies remain undiscovered for long periods of time – if they are found at all. Only around 13 % of the deceased1 are buried, most in nameless graves.

This is a persistent humanitarian crisis, in which many families are desperately waiting for answers that they are unlikely to ever receive. Despite the adoption of an EP resolution2 in 2021, there are hardly any EU or national mechanisms aimed at improving the identification of the deceased and the investigation of their deaths. This is an issue with human rights and moral implications. 1.
In what ways is the Commission empowered to take measures to guarantee the dignified recovery of the deceased and procedures for their proper identification?
With what measures, plans or financial resources is the Commission supporting procedures that could facilitate identification (e.g. the establishment of a transnational DNA database)?
answer: On 13 March 2024, the European Parliament and the Council adopted the Prüm II Regulation (EU) 2024/98 2 (3) on automated search and exchange of data for police cooperation. This regulation establishes a framework (the Prüm II framework) allowing Member States’ competent authorities to search and exchange specific data, such as DNA profiles, dactyloscopic data and facial images.

The purpose of the Prüm II framework is also to allow Member State’s competent authorities to search for missing persons in the context of criminal investigations or on humanitarian grounds and to identify human remains, provided that those authorities are empowered to conduct such searches and to carry out such identifications under national law.

Where Member States wish to use the Prüm II framework to search for missing persons outside the area of criminal investigations, Member States should adopt national legislative measures, laying down procedures, conditions and criteria clearly setting out the humanitarian grounds on which an automated search for missing persons can be conducted.
The humanitarian grounds should include natural and man-made disasters and other equally justified grounds.
